title: Start and end
summary: Anchors match positions: ^ and $, the Multiline flag that makes them per line, \A \z \Z, and the .NET rule that $ also matches before a final newline.

steps.title: Anchors match positions
body: Everything so far matched characters. An **anchor** matches a **position** between characters, and uses up none.
- `^` matches at the start of the text.
- `$` matches at the end of the text.
So `^ERROR` finds `ERROR` only when it is the very first thing. Below, the text has three lines but `^ERROR` finds
only the first one: without a flag, `^` means the start of the **whole text**, not of each line.
Now press the **m** flag (Multiline). `^` and `$` then match at the start and end of **every line**, and the third
line lights up too. Line-based tools like grep, rg and editor search always work this way.

steps.explain: `IsMatch` asks "is there a match **anywhere**?", and `123` is in there. With `^` and `$` the digits must run from the start to the end. This difference is behind a whole family of validation bugs (next lesson).

steps.title: Section headers in a config file
prompt: An INI file marks sections with a line like `[server]`. Find every section header: a `[`, lowercase letters and a
`]` at the **start of a line**. A value such as `name=[prod]` is not a header.
The input has several lines, so you will need the **m** flag.
hints: Without `^`, `name=[prod]` gives a match. Without the **m** flag, `^` only matches before `[server]`.
steps.explain: With Multiline, `^` matches after every newline. The brackets are escaped because `[` starts a class.

steps.title: Multiline, \A, \z, and the .NET $ trap
body: | `^` | start of text | start of text, and after every `\n` |
| `$` | end of text, **or before a final `\n`** | before every `\n`, and at the end |
| `\A` | start of text | start of text (never changes) |
| `\z` | end of text | end of text (never changes) |
| `\Z` | end, or before a final `\n` | same |
The row that catches people is `$`. In .NET (and Python, Perl, PCRE), `$` without `m` matches at the very end
**or just before a newline at the end**. So `^admin$` accepts `"admin\n"`. A trailing newline from a form field,
a file or a header can slip past a validator that way.
Rule of thumb: use `^` and `$` with **m** to work on lines; use `\A` and `\z` to mean the **whole** text. Note the
lower case: `\z` is the strict one, `\Z` allows the final newline.

steps.prompt: Match each anchor to where it matches in .NET.
pairs: only at the start of the text
at the start of every line
at the end, or just before a final newline
only at the very end, whatever the flags
at the end or before a final newline, whatever the flags
only at the start, whatever the flags

steps.title: TODO comments, and only real ones
prompt: Before a release you list every TODO comment. Find each line whose code starts with `// TODO`, possibly after
spaces or tabs of indentation, and match the whole line. A `// TODO` inside a string is not a comment.
Each match must be exactly the line, indentation included: `    // TODO: retry`.
hints: Start at the beginning of a line with `^`, allow indentation, then the literal `// TODO`, then the rest of the line.
Careful: `\s` also matches a newline, so `^\s*` can start on the blank line above. Use `[ \t]*`: `^[ \t]*// TODO.*`
steps.explain: `.*` stops at the end of the line because the dot does not match `\n`. `^\s*` finds the same lines, but the first match starts on the empty line and includes its newline: a classic surprise when the matches are printed or replaced.

steps.prompt: A sign-up form posts the user name with a trailing newline. What does this print?
steps.explain: `$` and `\Z` both allow one final newline. Only `\z` insists on the real end, so only it rejects `"admin\n"`.

steps.prompt: Complete the validator: a PIN is exactly four ASCII digits, and nothing else, not even a trailing newline.
steps.explain: At the start, `^` without m means the same as `\A`. At the end only `\z` refuses `"1234\n"`: `$` and `\Z` both accept it.

steps.title: Count the comment lines
prompt: Write `int CountComments(string config)`: how many lines of a config file are comments, meaning their first
non-blank character is `#`. Indentation is spaces or tabs. A `#` later in a line (`url=http://x/#top`) does not
Use `Regex.Count` with `RegexOptions.Multiline`, so that `^` matches at the start of every line.
Files may have Windows line endings (`\r\n`). `System.Text.RegularExpressions` is already imported.
template:
Dojo.Eq("two comments, one # inside a url", 2, CountComments("a=1
# c
  # indented
url=http://x/#top
"));
Dojo.Eq("a comment on the first line counts", 1, CountComments("#first\nb=2"));
Dojo.Eq("an empty file has none", 0, CountComments(""));
hints: The pattern is `^`, optional spaces or tabs, then `#`.
